subject: Physical Education
content:
TOPIC 7, SUBTOPIC A: VOLLEYBALL (Grade 7)

OBJECTIVES
Learners should be able to:
- demonstrate basic volleyball skills
- explain the basic rules of volleyball
- explain the rotation system used in volleyball
- identify common infringements in volleyball

BASIC SKILLS
1. Serving: the shot that starts each rally, hit from behind the court's back line.
- Underarm serve: the ball is held in one hand and struck with the other hand/fist from below, a simpler serve often taught to beginners.
- Overarm serve: the ball is tossed up and struck from above with an open hand or fist, generally faster but requiring more coordination.
2. Passing (the 'dig' or forearm pass): the two forearms are held together and used as a flat platform to control and direct a low or hard-hit ball upward to a teammate, usually the setter.
3. Setting: using the fingertips of both hands to push the ball gently and accurately upward and forward, typically to position it for a teammate to attack (spike).
4. Spiking (attacking hit): jumping and striking the ball forcefully with an open hand, aiming to hit it steeply downward into the opponent's court, usually finishing a team's attacking sequence.
5. Blocking: one or more players jumping at the net to intercept or deflect an opponent's attacking hit (spike) before it crosses into their own court.

BASIC RULES
- Each team is allowed up to three touches of the ball (not counting a block touch) before it must be returned over the net.
- The same player may not touch the ball twice in succession (except immediately after a block touch, in some rule variations).
- The ball must not touch the ground on a team's own side of the court; if it does, the opposing team wins the point/rally.
- A team wins the right to serve, and rotates positions clockwise by one position, each time they win a rally while not already serving.
- Matches are typically played in sets, with a team winning a set by reaching a set number of points (commonly 25, with a two-point lead required) first, though this can be simplified for school-level games.

THE ROTATION SYSTEM
Volleyball teams typically consist of six players arranged in two rows of three (front row and back row) on court. Whenever a team wins the serve (having just won a rally while receiving), all players rotate one position clockwise before the next serve. This ensures that all players take turns playing in different areas of the court, including at the net (front row) and further back (back row), over the course of a match.

COMMON INFRINGEMENTS
- Four hits: a team touching the ball four times before it crosses the net (illegal, since only three touches are allowed, not counting a block).
- Double hit: a single player touching the ball twice in a row illegally (e.g. an uncontrolled set that touches the hands twice).
- Net touch: a player touching the net during play, which is not allowed.
- Foot fault (on serve): stepping on or over the back line before or during the serve action.
- Carrying/lifting: catching, scooping or prolonged contact with the ball instead of a clean hit, which is not allowed.
- Reaching over the net: illegally reaching over the net to play the ball on the opponent's side, except in specific circumstances such as blocking an attacking hit already crossing into your side.

POSITIONS AND ROLES (BASIC OVERVIEW)
- Setter: usually responsible for the second touch, setting the ball accurately for attackers to spike.
- Outside/opposite hitters: primary attacking players, aiming to spike the ball set to them.
- Middle blockers: positioned near the centre of the net, focused on blocking opposing attacks and quick attacking plays.
- Libero (in more advanced/competitive play): a specialist defensive player who does not rotate to the front row and focuses on passing and digging, often wearing a different coloured shirt; this role may be simplified or omitted at school level.

SUMMARY
- Core volleyball skills include serving (underarm, overarm), passing/digging, setting, spiking and blocking.
- Teams are allowed up to three touches before returning the ball, and rotate positions clockwise after winning the serve.
- Common infringements include four hits, double hits, net touches, foot faults and carrying the ball.
- Basic roles include the setter (sets up attacks), hitters (attack/spike) and middle blockers (block and attack centrally).

GLOSSARY
Rally: the sequence of play from serve until a point is scored.
Rotation: the clockwise movement of players to a new court position after winning the serve.
Dig (forearm pass): using the forearms together to control and direct a hard-hit or low ball to a teammate.
source: Adapted from the ZIMSEC/Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education Junior (Grade 3-7) Physical Education, Sport and Mass Displays Syllabus (2015-2022), Topic 7

subject: Physical Education
content:
TOPIC 7, SUBTOPIC B: BADMINTON (Grade 7)

OBJECTIVES
Learners should be able to:
- demonstrate basic badminton skills
- explain the basic rules and scoring of badminton
- identify common shots used in badminton
- explain common infringements in badminton

EQUIPMENT AND COURT BASICS
Badminton is played with a lightweight racket and a shuttlecock (a cone-shaped object with feathers or synthetic material attached to a rounded cork or rubber base), across a net that divides the court in half. It can be played as singles (one player per side) or doubles (two players per side), with slightly different court boundary lines used for each.

BASIC SKILLS AND TECHNIQUE
1. Grip: the racket is usually held with a relaxed 'handshake grip', where the hand grips the handle as though shaking hands with it, allowing quick wrist movement for different shots.
2. Ready position: standing with knees slightly bent, weight balanced on the balls of the feet, racket held up in front of the body, ready to move quickly in any direction.
3. Footwork: quick, light steps used to move into position for each shot, then recovering back toward the centre of the court ('base position') after playing a shot.

COMMON SHOTS IN BADMINTON
- Serve: an underarm shot that starts each rally, hitting the shuttlecock diagonally into the correct service box on the opponent's side.
- Clear: a shot hit high and deep, aiming to land near the back of the opponent's court, often used to push an opponent backward and create time to recover position.
- Drop shot: a soft, gentle shot hit just over the net so the shuttlecock falls quickly and steeply into the front area of the opponent's court.
- Smash: a powerful, steeply downward attacking shot, usually played from an overhead position, aiming to win the point outright or force a weak return.
- Drive: a fast, flat shot travelling parallel to the ground, usually aimed at an opponent's body or into open space.
- Net shot: a delicate shot played very close to the net, aiming to just clear it and fall steeply on the opponent's side.

BASIC RULES AND SCORING
- A point is scored on every rally (rally-point scoring), regardless of which side served, in modern badminton rules.
- A game is typically won by the first side to reach 21 points, with at least a two-point lead required (subject to a points cap in some competition rules); matches are usually the best of three games.
- The shuttlecock must not touch the ground on your own side of the court, or the opposing side scores the point.
- The shuttlecock must land within the marked boundary lines relevant to the type of game being played (singles or doubles use slightly different side and back boundaries).
- Players/pairs alternate ends and serving responsibilities according to the score and specific serving rules for singles or doubles.

COMMON INFRINGEMENTS
- Shuttlecock landing outside the court boundary (out).
- Shuttlecock touching the ground on a player's own side before being returned (fault).
- Touching the net with the racket, body or clothing during play.
- Carrying or double-hitting the shuttlecock instead of a single, clean strike.
- Foot faults during service, such as stepping outside the correct service box area before or during the serve.

TACTICS SPECIFIC TO BADMINTON
- Using a clear to push an opponent to the back of the court, then following with a drop shot to the front, forcing the opponent to cover the whole court and tire quickly.
- Using a smash when the shuttlecock is high, to attack aggressively and win the point outright.
- Returning to the central base position after every shot, to be ready to reach the next shot from any direction.

SUMMARY
- Badminton is played with a racket and shuttlecock over a net, in singles or doubles format.
- Key shots include the serve, clear, drop shot, smash, drive and net shot.
- Games are typically played to 21 points (rally-point scoring, requiring a two-point lead), best of three games.
- Common infringements include the shuttlecock landing out, touching the ground on your own side, and net touches.
- Good tactics combine clears and drops to move an opponent around the court, and smashes to attack when the shuttlecock is high.

GLOSSARY
Rally-point scoring: a scoring system where a point is awarded on every rally, regardless of which side served.
Smash: a powerful, steeply downward attacking shot in badminton.
Base position: the central court position a badminton player returns to after playing a shot, ready to move to the next one.
source: Adapted from the ZIMSEC/Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education Junior (Grade 3-7) Physical Education, Sport and Mass Displays Syllabus (2015-2022), Topic 7

subject: Physical Education
topic: Net Games: General Tactics and Values
content:
TOPIC 7, SUBTOPIC C: GENERAL TACTICS AND VALUES IN NET GAMES (Grade 7)

OBJECTIVES
Learners should be able to:
- explain common tactical principles shared across net games
- apply simple placement and variation tactics during play
- explain the importance of court positioning and recovery
- describe the values developed through participation in net games

WHAT DO NET GAMES HAVE IN COMMON?
Although volleyball and badminton use different equipment and skills, they share the same core tactical structure: a net divides two sides, and each side attempts to send an object over the net in a way the opponent cannot successfully return, while defending their own side of the court. Because of this, several tactical principles apply across all net games.

SHARED TACTICAL PRINCIPLES
1. Placement: aiming shots or hits toward open or difficult-to-reach areas of the opponent's court (such as the corners or the space between two opposing players), rather than always hitting directly at an opponent, who can then return the shot more easily.
2. Variation: mixing up the type, height, pace and direction of shots (for example, alternating between a hard, fast shot and a soft, gentle one) to prevent an opponent from predicting and preparing for the next shot.
3. Depth: using shots that push an opponent deep into their own court (such as a clear in badminton or a well-placed serve in volleyball) can create space at the front of the court to exploit with a following shot.
4. Recovery/base position: after playing a shot, quickly returning to a central, balanced 'ready' position allows a player to reach the widest possible range of return shots.
5. Reading the opponent: watching an opponent's body position and racket/arm preparation can give clues about where their next shot is likely to go, allowing a player to react more quickly.
6. Teamwork and communication (for team net games like volleyball): calling for the ball clearly, communicating who will play a shot near a shared area of responsibility, and supporting teammates after they play a shot.

APPLYING TACTICS DURING PLAY
When playing simplified or small-sided net games in class, learners should practise:
- choosing where to aim a shot based on where the opponent is standing, rather than hitting the same way every time
- deciding when to play a safe, controlled shot to keep the rally going versus when to attempt a more attacking, risky shot to win the point
- moving back to a ready, central position immediately after every shot

WHY COURT POSITIONING MATTERS
Good court positioning reduces the distance a player has to move to reach the next shot, saves energy over a long match or rally, and reduces the chance of being caught out of position by a well-placed opponent's shot. Learners who consistently return to a sensible base position after each shot will generally cover the court more effectively than those who remain wherever their last shot left them.

VALUES AND SKILLS DEVELOPED THROUGH NET GAMES
- Hand-eye coordination: judging and reacting to a moving ball or shuttlecock requires well-developed coordination, which improves with regular practice.
- Concentration: net games often involve fairly long rallies where a single lapse in focus can cost a point, encouraging sustained attention.
- Patience and tactical thinking: success often comes from patiently building an advantage through placement and variation rather than trying to win every point with maximum power immediately.
- Honesty and fair play: many net games, especially in informal or school settings, rely on players honestly calling whether a shot landed in or out, building integrity and self-regulation.
- Physical fitness: the frequent, quick movements required in net games develop agility, speed and general fitness.

SUMMARY
- Net games share core tactical principles: placement, variation, depth, recovery to a base position, reading the opponent, and (for team games) communication.
- Applying these tactics during play involves deciding where to aim shots and when to play safely versus attacking.
- Good court positioning and quick recovery to a base position help a player cover the court efficiently.
- Net games build coordination, concentration, patience, honesty and physical fitness.

GLOSSARY
Placement: deliberately aiming a shot toward a specific area of the court, usually one that is difficult for the opponent to reach.
Variation: deliberately changing the type, pace, height or direction of shots to make play unpredictable for an opponent.
Base position: a central, balanced position a player returns to after each shot, allowing quick movement to the next shot.
source: Adapted from the ZIMSEC/Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education Junior (Grade 3-7) Physical Education, Sport and Mass Displays Syllabus (2015-2022), Topic 7
